Sources: NYU Law Library Bloomberg Getting Started function directory; University of Scranton (Kania School) Bloomberg Training Booklet, 67pp; professional.bloomberg.com/support/documentation (hardware/IT specs only — not training); @ObjectiveTrade, full channel, 20 transcripts (~288k words) — a former options/equity trader screen-recording a live seat, then, after losing access, screen-recording the substitutes. Second pull (workflow-targeted): Damodaran's own In Practice webcast on using a Terminal for valuation data; Bloomberg's official Terminal Essentials: Fixed Income; an FA-screen walkthrough; a live pair-trade build; two trading-floor documentaries. Synthesized, not reproduced. Raw corpus at _ingest/raw/2026-09-26/; searchable function index published separately as an artifact (link in §9).

Why this note exists: the program has a data layer (sec filing intelligence, _ingest/edgar.py) and a judgment layer (acumen/), but no note on instrumentation — the tooling between them, and what its absence costs. This matters because sec filing intelligence makes a claim this note partially refutes (§3), and because acumen/MECHANISM.md needs a way to ask whether a scored call depended on data the analyst could not have had. Maps to Course 01 (Accounting), Course 02 (Corporate Finance & Valuation), Course 07 (Data & Decision-Making), Course 11 (Global Strategy & Macro), and E8 (Investor Relations).

Provenance: §§1–2 and §5–8 are from the sources. §3 is this note's own argument and is not in any source — it is a direct disagreement with an existing repo note. §4 is the map, built by pairing the function index against learn/ units and CURRICULUM.md; §5 carries its own evidence grades. Prices are as captured and will drift.

1 · Three witnesses, opposite ends of a $30,000 gap, same verdict

sec filing intelligence states the program's position on professional terminals in one line:

"Proprietary terminals (Bloomberg, FactSet) add analytical layers but the underlying filings are the same public data."

That note reaches this from the outside, reasoning about the corpus. Two further witnesses reach it from inside a seat. First, ObjectiveTrade, more bluntly:

"All the information is available to you elsewhere." — and, on retail use: "You don't need it. It is complete overkill."

He is not a free-tools evangelist making a virtue of necessity. He had institutional access at an options fund, made twenty videos demonstrating the platform, then lost the seat and spent the next several videos testing what replaces it. His answer, after auditing Refinitiv/XENITH at $150/mo, Godel at $60, Money.Net Scout at $12–60, OpenBB at zero, and stockanalysis.com at ~$5, was to settle on the $5/mo option for long-horizon equity research — the same tier of tool this repo already operates above with a free EDGAR CLI.

And then a third witness, who matters more than either — Aswath Damodaran, this program's named source for Course 01 and Course 02, in his own In Practice webcast, recorded from a live Terminal:

"Almost all of the data here is public data, there's very little private information. You could pretty much get the same data elsewhere — it will be a lot more work." … "The data that's on Bloomberg is available elsewhere for the most part, and you should be able to get that data as well."

This is convergent validation of the program's core bet. Three independent parties — one paying ~$30k/yr, one paying nothing, and the academic the curriculum already cites — agree that Layer 1 is a commodity and that the analytical value sits above it. The EDGAR×event pedagogy in learn/ is not a budget approximation of a professional workflow. It is the same Layer 1, read directly instead of through a vendor.

Damodaran goes further, and his extra step is the sharpest thing in the whole corpus. Bloomberg now computes cost of capital and equity risk premium for you. He refuses to use them:

"I don't trust the numbers that Bloomberg comes up with — not because the people behind the numbers are not smart people with access to data, but because it's incredibly opaque. You have no idea what goes on behind the number… I use Bloomberg to get raw data. I think it's my job in corporate finance and valuation to estimate things like equity risk premiums and costs of capital."

That is sec filing intelligence's three-layer stack restated by a practitioner: take Layer 1, refuse someone else's Layer 3, build your own. A $30k instrument's most convenient outputs are the ones the most credible user in the field declines, on explainability grounds — the same grounds that note calls the deepest structural property of filing-derived intelligence. The convenience is the trap; the raw data is the product.

2 · What the $30,000 buys, precisely

A bare-bones seat runs ~$25,000–30,000/yr (delayed quotes, limited broker research); volume pricing lands near $26–27k; real-time exchange data and research are extra. Four things justify it, and only one of them is data.

1. Aggregation — the purchase is time, not information. Every item the program pulls from EDGAR, FRED, and agency sites is one command away instead of one workflow away. This is the honest core of the value proposition and all three witnesses say so.

2. Cross-asset grammar. The yellow-key system (F2 government, F3 corporate, F8 equity, F9 commodity, F11 currency) means one syntax covers every asset class. DES describes a bond, a stock, a future or a currency pair depending on which key preceded it. The free stack has no equivalent: you learn EDGAR for equities, FRED for rates, TRACE for corporate bonds, and a broker platform for options, each with its own model of the world. This, not any individual dataset, is the largest genuine capability gap — and it is the reason Course 11 (Global Strategy & Macro) and E9 are the hardest courses to instrument freely.

3. Data EDGAR genuinely does not contain. The table below is the honest inventory. "Free substitute" is graded against what this repo can actually reach today.

Terminal capability Fn Free substitute Grade
Consensus estimates, per-analyst ratings & price targets ANR EEO EE Aggregated consensus on stockanalysis / Yahoo; Scout (~$60/mo) gives named analysts with individual accuracy records Partial
Credit ratings with outlook, consolidated CRPR RATC Agency sites + issuer press releases, one at a time Partial, laborious
Modelled default probability DRSK None. Altman-Z is computable by hand from edgar.py facts Substitutable by work
CDS pricing, single-name & sovereign CDS SOVR WCDS None No
Option volatility surface / term structure OVDV OMON Chains free on thinkorswim; no surface Partial
Short interest & float % SI SIA FINRA biweekly, Finviz Mostly yes, lagged
Block trades, dealer inventory, IOIs MBTR AQR IMGR None No
Supply-chain graph (suppliers ↔ customers with revenue exposure) SPLC 10-K Item 1 major-customer disclosure + segment concentration, assembled manually per company Partial, expensive
Bond terms & pricing across ~400k active issues SRCH YAS FINRA TRACE (prices, no analytics) Partial
Real-time quotes, Level II, time & sales BQ thinkorswim, free with a funded account Yes
Physical-flow alt data: tankers, pipelines, refineries, rigs, transmission lines, outages BMAP MAP Scattered, mostly paid No
The messaging network IB None at any price No

Note the shape of it: the gaps are concentrated in credit, derivatives, flow, and physical commodities — precisely the domains learn/ does not cover and CURRICULUM.md treats lightly. For equity fundamentals, which is where this program actually operates, the free stack is close to complete.

4. The network. IB (Instant Bloomberg) is an unremarkable chat client containing nearly everyone in institutional finance. Deals are transacted on it. Both sources identify this — not data quality — as the reason nobody has displaced Bloomberg. (Compliance note: IB and MSG traffic is logged in full and readable by your firm; several banks' group-chat scandals were sourced from it.)

Cross-link worth making explicit. sec filing intelligence closes on the Moat Paradox: the raw material is a public good, so the moat migrates upward to extraction, then judgment, then niche authority — "when a specific community of decision-makers adopts your judgment framework as their standard lens, the framework becomes infrastructure rather than product." That note cites Cboe/VIX as the example. Bloomberg is the same mechanism at full scale, and it landed one layer higher still: not a framework the community adopted, but the interface the community adopted. The moat is neither the data nor the analytics — it is that the mnemonics, the keyboard, and the chat client became the profession's shared vocabulary. Godel's strategy is the tell: it deliberately copies Bloomberg's command grammar (DES, FA, HDS, EQS) because the switching cost it must beat is muscle memory, not features. Straight canon helmer 7 powers switching costs layered on network economies.

3 · Where this note disagrees with the repo

sec filing intelligence lists "public access" as a compliance property producing this intelligence capability:

"No information-asymmetry barrier — the raw material is free and identical for every analyst, from a solo operator to Goldman Sachs."

That is true about the corpus and false about the clock, and the distinction is load-bearing.

Information symmetry is a claim about content. It says nothing about latency. Consider one fact — a large institution repositioning out of a name:

Observer Sees it via When
Bloomberg seat MBTR / AQR block print Seconds
Bloomberg seat SI short-interest change Biweekly
This repo 13F via FLNG equivalent / EDGAR Up to 45 days after quarter-end

Same fact, same legal disclosure regime, same public corpus — a latency spread of roughly seven weeks. For a compounder holding five years, seven weeks is noise and the symmetry claim holds completely. For any decision with a clock on it — a credit event, a rate decision, an earnings reaction, a merger spread — seven weeks is the entire trade, and the playing field is not level in any sense the word normally carries.

The corrected formulation: the SEC filing system equalizes access to the historical record and does nothing to equalize access to the present. This repo's chosen ground — long-horizon fundamental analysis, learn/ through acumen/ — sits almost entirely in the historical record, which is why the free stack works here and why it would not work on a trading desk. That is a deliberate strategic position, and it is stronger for being stated rather than assumed. It also draws the boundary of the program honestly: this curriculum does not teach, and cannot instrument, anything where latency is the edge.

Recommended as an addendum to sec filing intelligence's "Public access" row rather than a contradiction of it — the property is real, its scope was overstated.

5 · Workflows, graded by evidence

A correction first. The three desk workflows originally published with this research — equity analyst, credit, macro-morning — were my ordering of functions, not observed practice. The primary practitioner source is explicit that he had no plan ("I didn't have a written plan for how I was going to do this, I just thought I was going to show you some of the functions I use"), and Parts 2 and 3 are structured as addenda. He closes Part 3 by proposing exactly the missing artifact —

"What I might do is sort of take you through flow of what an equity analyst or an equity trader might do during a day at work."

— and never made it. The channel goes on to PORT, Launchpad, backtesting, maps and XLTP instead. The single largest gap in the original corpus was the thing its own author identified and left open. A second, workflow-targeted pull closed most of it. Current grades:

5a · Damodaran's data pull — the one that plugs straight into Course 02

  1. WEI as the landing page.
  2. Type the company name, disambiguate to the local listing (MSFT US Equity), land on the entry page.
  3. HDS — largest holders. He flags the provenance himself: sourced from SEC filings, nothing proprietary.
  4. BETA — and the point is that it returns the regression, not just a number. Defaults are parochial: a US stock against the S&P 500, a German one against the DAX, two years of weekly returns. Every amber field is editable — swap the index to MSCI World, weekly → monthly, two years → five, and it re-runs on the spot.
  5. FA — the statements.
  6. SOVR — sovereign CDS spreads, which is where his published country-default-spread methodology sources its input.
  7. Stop. Do not take WACC or the computed ERP (§1).

Works on obscure names, which is the part students disbelieve: he demonstrates on Vinamilk (VNM Vietnamese Equity) and gets holders and a beta regression.

5b · The credit workflow, corrected

What was published was constructed. The real sequence, from Bloomberg's own training material, routes through market context first and execution last, and uses six functions the constructed version lacked entirely:

  1. FICM — fixed income credit monitor. The dashboard: spreads by instrument and sector, filter to investment grade / high yield / emerging markets, drill into a sector.
  2. WB — world bonds. Yield and spread deviation from the average, to pinpoint anomalies worth investigating. The RMI column flags significant moves in related markets.
  3. BBTI — commonly traded rates, sorted by category: outright, forwards, curves, butterflies.
  4. SRCH — and it takes natural language. Typing "US corporate retail amount outstanding greater than 500 million" is parsed into search parameters.
  5. Export → FIW, the fixed income worksheet. Subset by asset class, currency, maturity; chart it to surface outliers.
  6. COMB — comparable bond analysis. Is this issue rich or cheap against similar issuance?
  7. YAS — yield and spread. The spreads are clickable and adjustable, so yield calculations can be tested live.
  8. ALLQ — every pricing source and contributing counterparty you are entitled to, aggregated into one relative-value screen.
  9. IMGR — quotes already received, including over IB, consolidated.

PCS sets your pricing source once, globally, across all of the above.

5c · The detail that should change how this repo teaches

Inside FA, clicking any line item drills down — and the drill-down links back to the original 10-K, with management's own explanation adjacent. The worked example in the source: Disney's interest expense falls three straight years; click through; the filing says the decrease was driven by higher capitalised interest from the Shanghai Disney Resort development.

That is EDGAR × event, inside the Terminal, as a single click. The program's core pedagogy is a Bloomberg feature. Which is the strongest possible argument that learn/'s four-pillar model is aimed correctly — and a reminder that what the Terminal sells here is, again, only the click.

6 · Breaks when — the terminal is corrosive to this pedagogy if introduced early

The house template demands a failure-mode section. This one is sharp, because the failure is not technical.

learn/README.md rule 2: "Show every computation as a step, not a result." The four-pillar model works because the beginner computes the ugly number themselves — Unit 04 makes you divide $30.9B by $2.9B and feel 10.7× before it tells you the company nearly died. FA renders that as a lookup. The number arrives correct, pre-formatted, and meaningless. Aggregation removes exactly the friction that builds the understanding. A student who learns the health check on a terminal has learned where a screen is, not what leverage is.

The rule this implies, stated in the same register as the existing one:

Keep the core Application terminal-free. Any Bloomberg function is a clearly-labeled optional extra, the same way edgar.py already is. Arc A must be completed by hand.

BT is the sharper trap. Backtesting is four clicks and produces a chart of a strategy that worked. The channel's own worked example is the perfect artifact: a Bollinger mean-reversion rule on 3M, 2010–2021, returned 133% — which reads as a success until you run TRA on the same ticker over the same window and find that buying at the first entry and never trading again returned 134% on price alone and 215% with dividends. The strategy underperformed doing nothing by 82 points, and the interface presents it as a win, because the interface has no opinion about the counterfactual.

This is canon mauboussin success equation (the luck/skill continuum, and the failure to specify a base rate) and canon kahneman thinking fast and slow (WYSIATI — the result on screen is the whole world) rendered as a UI affordance. It also belongs with canon taleb black swan on backfitting a narrative to a sample. Fold into quant-backtesting/ as the worked cautionary case; the discipline it teaches is always compute the do-nothing counterfactual before reading the strategy result, which generalizes far past trading.

A third, quieter one. Bloomberg Intelligence (BI, BICO) hands you a staff analyst's industry read. It is good. It is also someone else's framing arriving before you have formed your own, which is the mechanism acumen/MECHANISM.md is built to defeat — the "unprompted crux rate" input measures precisely the ability to name the crux before it is handed to you. Read BI after your memo, never before.

7 · What this gives acumen/ — a constraint audit, not more corpus

acumen/MECHANISM.md is explicit that corpus size is not an input metric and names "24 modules, 82 books, 352 cross-links" as vanity measurement. A note contributing 210 function codes would be exactly that. So the contribution here is a rubric input instead.

Proposed red-team question, for the case template:

Did this call depend on data the analyst could not have obtained — and if so, was the dependency acknowledged?

Three outcomes, each scoring differently:

Finding Reading
Call rests only on filing-derivable data Clean. The historical-record ground this program occupies
Call rests on terminal-only data (§2 table) and says so, with a stated assumption Acceptable — the uncertainty is priced
Call rests on terminal-only data and doesn't notice Failure. A confident memo resting on a number the analyst assumed was knowable

The third is the valuable catch, and it is invisible without §2's inventory. It is also a specific, countable version of the calibration-error input the mechanism already tracks: a call that silently requires CDS spreads or block-trade flow is not an uncertain call, it is an unfounded one, and the distinction should cost different points.

8 · Access — the cheapest real move

You do not have to decide between $30,000 and nothing.

University Bloomberg labs. Most business schools run them; accounts are free, licensed to the hardware, and require only a mobile number for two-factor at signup. The session does not leave the building without Bloomberg Anywhere, which is a further charge. On macOS the Terminal runs through Citrix Workspace, not natively.

BESS — Bloomberg Market Concepts / Essentials. Free from any terminal: video modules on equities, fixed income, FX and commodities, an exam per module, 75% earns an Acknowledgement of Completion. It is the one credential in reach of this program that a recruiter recognizes on sight, and the program's own rubric treats credential-free self-study as a weakness to manage. BPS holds the cheat sheets, SMNR runs daily 20–30 minute webinars, JOBS lists roles posted only inside the Terminal.

The deliberate buy, if any. Ranked by marginal value to this program specifically:

Tool Cost Buys you Verdict for this repo
stockanalysis.com Pro ~$5–8/mo 270+ screener filters, 10–40yr financials, spreadsheet export The rational purchase. Compresses edgar.py facts workflows and adds screening the repo lacks
Godel Terminal ~$60/mo Bloomberg command grammar, linked panels, Excel export Buy only to learn the grammar cheaply before a lab session
Money.Net Scout ~$12–60/mo Named analysts with individual accuracy records The one genuinely distinctive item at this tier
MetaStock XENITH ~$150/mo Refinitiv, stripped; strong Reuters news Poor fit — many functions return "not privileged"
OpenBB free Open-source CLI over third-party APIs Already duplicated by _ingest/edgar.py, and less reliable
